notes: The owner's words: "I want to know the newsworthiness test and whether or not um, local and state and federal stuff all follow the same thing."
question: ChatGPT's A07 answer set out what makes an event worth printing and said outlets differ in scope, beat, audience and sources. The owner asks the narrower follow-up directly: should local, state and federal coverage follow the same newsworthiness test, or does the test itself differ by level of government? Specifically: (1) which criteria are shared across levels and which change (for example, does a town council vote clear a local paper's bar on a lower threshold of affected people than a state capitol paper uses); (2) whether the same event should be scored separately at each level it touches, so a local story can escalate to state or national coverage; and (3) what real editorial practice at local, state-capitol and national outlets says about the difference.

title: Does one newsworthiness test apply to local, state and federal news
usableAnswer: A per-level statement of the newsworthiness criteria (local, state, federal), saying which are shared and which differ, with an escalation rule for when an event at one level becomes a story at another. A ruling that one test with outlet-specific thresholds is enough is also a complete answer.
whyItMatters: The press desk scores every public event with one weekly formula across all outlets. If the test should differ by level, that is a structural change to how stories are picked, not a tuning of weights, and it decides whether a player's local actions ever reach a state or national paper.

answer.summary: One test, applied by each outlet, with no universal score. Record the event once (place, people, office, stakes, evidence); stories read that event and never create facts. Each outlet decides whether it can learn and verify it and whether it fits its audience, beat and space, using shared terms: consequence, timeliness, accountability, novelty, conflict, human stakes. A town paper covers what directly affects its residents; a state outlet picks a story up for state policy, many communities, state officials or a pattern; a national outlet for federal action, broad consequence, national figures, precedent or a cross-state pattern; stories also move down as local outlets localize federal news. Syndication and follow-ups keep provenance. Owner decision: reach helps a newsroom discover a story; broader relevance and editorial judgment decide national coverage, and attention alone never triggers it. Places with little press still have outlets, and a missing municipal government does not erase a local paper. Sources: AP News Values, AP's 2020 statehouse network, AP 'When national becomes local', Pew 2015, ProPublica's Local Reporting Network.
answer.stillOpen: Pending lamontae: whether there is any numeric threshold. Sources give no numeric thresholds or outlet coverage probabilities; newsroom capacity, syndication and beats vary.
